This pool is located near Cottonwood Campground on the North Kaibab Trail in Grand Canyon National Park.
Cottonwood Campground (CCG) is a small campground 6.8 miles below the North Rim of the Grand Canyon on the North Kaibab Trail. 
To camp in this campground you must obtain a backcountry permit. www.nps.gov/grca/planyourvisit/backcountry-permit.htm
Every campsite at Cottonwood Campground has a picnic table, pack pole, and metal food storage can. All food, toiletries, and plastics must be placed inside the food storage can.

Bright Angel Creek nearby offers a cool and refreshing place to get wet. Seasonally (mid-May to mid-Oct) potable drinking water is available at the campground. During other times of the year you should be prepared to filter/treat water obtained from the creek. There are deer, ringtail cats, and squirrels in the area. 

At Cottonwood Campgrouned, there is an emergency phone, and toilets. Day hike destinations include Roaring Springs, Ribbon Falls, and Manzanita Canyon. NPS video.

meta.credit: Fossil Lake
meta.description:
View of sand dunes and vegetation at Fossil Lake, with the Christmas Valley Sand Dunes and Lost Forest in the background, Feb. 21, 2017, by Greg Shine, BLM.
The Fossil Lake Area of Critical Environmental Concern includes the dry lake bed of Fossil Lake, once the bottom of an ancient lake more than 200 feet deep, and an area that - since 1877 - continues to be an important location for scientific discovery.
Over more than 100 years, paleontologists identified over 23 species of mammals, 74 species of birds, 6 species of fish, and 6 species of mollusk from fossils unearthed here. 
Some species are extinct, such as the mammoth, Dire wolf, giant beaver, and a large species of eagle. Others, such as the Tui chub, rabbit, ground squirrel, salmon, and prairie dog, exist here or in other parts of North America. 
These fossils range in age from about 10,000 years old, to as much as 400,000 years old. 
Each year, new species continue to be unearthed by research groups at Fossil Lake.

Photographed on April 20, 2013 on the Tonto Platform in Grand Canyon National Park. The vast expanse of the Tonto Platform is located approximately 3900 ft (1200 m) below the South Rim, and separates the inner gorge from the outer gorge of the canyon. 
Grand Canyon Park is home to hundreds of flowering plants. There are approximately 650 herbaceous (having little or no woody stem) wildflowers in the park. 
Some of the common species displaying a white flower are the sacred datura, evening primrose, tidy fleabane, yarrow, baby white aster, desert tobacco, watercress, and white violet. 
Some common yellow flowering wildflowers are broom snakeweed, yellow ragweed, hymenopapus, groundcherry, common mullein, Hooker's primrose, and blanket flower. 
Red or orange flowered plants include the globe mallow, red columbine, skyrocket, penstemon, Indian paintbrush, and crimson monkeyflower. 

Pink and purple wildflowers include the Rocky Mountain bee plant, fleabane, Palmer lupine, toadflax penstemon, Grand Canyon phacelia, and Rocky Mountain iris.

meta.description:
Not long after the 1989 wildfire season, the BLM began an effort to restore native Willamette Valley prairie lands via prescribed burning.
This vintage video, from 1989, shows one effort in Eugene, Oregon, that involved multiple partners: Army Corps of Engineers; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; the Nature Conservancy; and Oregon State University.
The goal, according to BLM Botanist Peter Zika in the video, was to restore the area to what it looked like when the first pioneers arrived on the Oregon Trail.
“They arrived here in the Willamette Valley and what they saw was 2,000 square miles of prairie that looked just like this, but without the trees; and with the fire, what we’re going to do is restore it to that original condition,” said Zika in the 26-year-old video.
